Flood Insurance Data

Peak month of NFIP claims by county

In plain words

In 404 of the 416 listed counties, over half of the busiest month's NFIP claims (losses 2016–2025) came in a single year. The busiest month is the month of the year with the most claims over 2016–2025; this does not say whether it floods in other years. In the median listed county the busiest month held 56.9% of claims.

Find your county (416 listed; a county with fewer than 100 NFIP claims with a month of loss is not):

In FEMA's records for losses 2016–2025, across the 416 counties with at least 100 NFIP claims with a month of loss each, 69.9% (90% range 66.4–72.7%, resampling counties) of those claims fell in their county's peak month; had each county's claims fallen at random, each of the twelve months equally likely, 9.3% would be expected to; the largest of twelve months always holds at least a twelfth.

By Michael Woo, publisher of Flood Insurance Data (about the site), who works with data, is not an insurance agent, adjuster or engineer, and answers for every figure here. Written with AI tools; every row is recomputed from FEMA's records by a separate check before publishing. First published 2026-11-13; data as of August 31, 2026.

Abstract

Main finding: In 404 of the 416 counties the peak month has at least 10 claims and one year holds over half of them. That mark does not say whether the month floods in other years. Graded instead, the median county's largest loss year holds 95.5% of its peak month (the earlier month where two tie), and that month has 10 or more claims in 1 of the 10 loss years at the median county.

Data: 416 counties with at least 100 NFIP claims with a month of loss each (515,295 in all), from FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP Claims v3, losses 2016–2025, as of August 31, 2026.

Result: across those counties, 69.9% (90% range 66.4–72.7%, resampling counties) of NFIP claims with a month of loss fell in their county's peak month, against 9.3% expected at random; the median county's share is 56.9%, against a median expected share at random of 11.3% (each county at its own claim count). Ranked by share minus that expectation, the largest excess is Monroe County, FL: 98.8% against 8.8% expected at random (8,529 of 8,636); its peak month is September, and over half of those claims are from September 2017 alone; the smallest is Dallas County, TX: 19.0% against 10.6% expected at random (90 of 473).

Question

In which month of the year do a U.S. county's NFIP flood claims most often fall, how much larger is that month's share than claims spread at random would give, and how much of that month is one year's claims? The measure is the share of a county's NFIP claims, paid or not, whose date of loss falls in the county's peak month (the month of the year with the most claims there).

Most NFIP policies take effect 30 days after you buy, so a policy bought today will not cover a flood this week.

Data

FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP Claims v3 (API) records as of August 31, 2026, FEMA fields dateOfLoss, yearOfLoss, countyCode, nonPaymentReasonBuilding. Base: NFIP claims on every building type, paid or not, with a loss year in the window and a month in the date of loss, the month read from the date as FEMA writes it (no time-zone shift); records FEMA coded deleted or assigned in error (nonPaymentReasonBuilding 98 and 99) left out.

FEMA defines dateOfLoss as "Date on which water first entered the insured building. When time is not specified in the field, it will default to T00:00:00.000Z".

FEMA defines yearOfLoss as "Year in which the flood loss occurred".

FEMA defines countyCode as "FIPS code uniquely identifying the primary County (e.g., 011 represents Broward County) associated with the project. Note, the County Code field may not reflect the individual county the property is located as projects can be associated with more than one county".

Methods

The share is the number of NFIP claims with a month of loss that fell in their county's peak month, divided by all NFIP claims with a month of loss in the county FEMA codes on the record, both counted from the same records. A county is listed only with at least 100 NFIP claims with a month of loss. Left out: 2,104 counties with fewer than 100 NFIP claims with a month of loss and 507 with none; across the 2,104 left-out counties with at least one, the median share of claims in the peak month is 54.9% and the pooled share 54.3%, so the listed counties are not a sample of every county. The expected share at random is, for each county, the mean share of the largest month over 4,000 draws of the county's own number of claims spread at random over twelve equally likely months (seeded by that number, so it reruns exactly); counties are ranked and put in fifths by share minus that expectation, in percentage points, and an equal excess always gets the same fifth. Intervals, fifths, the county-resampling range, records left out and why no test is run: shared methods for every paper.

Results

  • Pooled over the 416 counties: 69.9% (90% range 66.4–72.7%) of 515,295 NFIP claims with a month of loss, against 9.3% expected at random; the 2,104 counties left out pool to 54.3%.
  • Peak month by county: September in 113, August in 74, October in 50 of the 416 counties (ties count each month); in 404 of them over half of the peak month is one year.
  • Median county: 56.9%, against a median expected share at random of 11.3%. Largest excess over chance: Monroe County, FL, 98.8% (90% range if claims were independent 98.5–98.9%) against 8.8% expected at random.
  • 11 of the 50 counties with the largest excess over chance in claims in the peak month are in Florida, which has 44 of the 416 listed counties.

Prior work

No published ranking or table of U.S. counties by the calendar month of NFIP flood claims was found in searches on 2026-11-13 (WebSearch: NFIP flood claims by month of loss by county peak month; flood season by county NFIP claims seasonality map; dateOfLoss NFIP claims seasonality month analysis county). County tables of NFIP claims found in those searches count claims by year of loss, not by month.

All 416 counties

Largest excess over chance first; counties with a page on this site are linked. The 90% ranges are narrower than they should be for two reasons: the peak month is picked from the same claims it is measured on, and claims from one flood are not independent, most of all in the marked rows, where one year holds over half of the peak month. Each range is the one that would hold if claims were independent.

Limitations

  • Each county's 90% range is narrower than it should be for two reasons: the peak month is picked from the same claims it is measured on, so the share is the highest of twelve by construction (the expected share at random, beside each row, shows how much of it chance alone gives), and claims from one flood are not independent, which matters most in the marked rows where one year holds over half of the peak month. The ranges are those that would hold if claims were independent.
  • A marked row means only that one year holds over half of the peak month's claims; that year may hold one flood or several. The mark does not say whether the month floods in other years and almost every listed county has one; the columns beside it give the largest year's share of the peak month and two counts of loss years with claims in it.
  • A large excess over chance can come from one flood event: one storm's claims, all in one month, raise both the share and the excess.
  • The expectation at random treats the twelve months as equally likely and ignores their different numbers of days.
  • Claims count insured buildings that filed, not floods: one storm can bring thousands of claims, and a flood where few buildings are insured brings few.
  • Ten loss years are a short record: a month with few or no claims here can still flood.
  • Counties are those FEMA codes on the claim, which can differ from the property's county.
  • Only NFIP records: private flood insurance is not in FEMA's data.
  • A fifth is a position in this list, not a grade, a risk score or a prediction.

Reproduce

Download every record from FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP Claims v3, keep the NFIP claims with a month of loss for losses 2016–2025, group by the county FEMA codes, count the base and the records meeting the measure, drop counties under 100, and compute each share of claims in the peak month with a 90% Wilson interval (z = 1.64485), checking against the CSV, which gives every numerator and denominator. Then compute each county's expected peak share at random as in Methods and rank on share minus it; the CSV gives both.

How to cite

Michael Woo, Flood Insurance Data, "Peak month of NFIP claims by county," NFIP losses 2016–2025, data as of August 31, 2026, https://floodinsurancedata.com/flood-insurance/flood-calendar/. This product uses FEMA's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Versions

This is a fixed copy of the version with data as of August 31, 2026; it is not changed by later refreshes. The current version has the latest data.

Corrections

  • 2026-11-14: Excess over chance is now the printed share minus the printed expected share. One county changed: Taylor County, FL (12123), from 56.5 to 56.4 points. No county changed rank or fifth.

Report a figure that looks wrong to contact@floodinsurancedata.com; every correction is listed here with its date.
